title: Compliance and safety
summary: How to run ads that follow platform policy and local law, make honest claims, respect privacy and keep your accounts and money safe. Regulated verticals like trading and gambling reward buyers who play it straight, and this module shows what that looks like day to day.

lessons.title: How ad policies work
objectives: By the end you can explain how ads are reviewed before and while they run.
By the end you can tell allowed, restricted and prohibited content apart.
By the end you can explain why regulated verticals need authorization.

steps.h: Every platform has rules for ads
steps.p: Meta, TikTok, Google and Snapchat each publish advertising policies. They say what you may promote, how you may say it and who you may show it to. Every ad you submit is checked against them.

d.s: An ad that breaks the rules never gets to prove itself

steps.say: Every major platform has rules for ads. Meta, TikTok, Google and Snapchat each publish advertising policies. They say what you may promote, how you may say it, and who you may show it to. Every ad you submit is checked against them. That's why we say policy first, creative second. An ad that breaks the rules never gets to prove itself.

steps.h: The life of an ad in review
steps.p: Review is not a single gate. Ads are checked when submitted, mostly by automated systems and sometimes by people, and they can be checked again at any time while they run.
d: Submit ad
Automated review
Approved or rejected
Checked again while live
Appeal if you think it is wrong
steps.more: Because ads are re-checked while live, an ad that was approved yesterday can be rejected today, and a pattern of rejections can affect the whole ad account. Reviews also look at the landing page, not just the ad itself. If the page breaks a rule, the ad can be rejected even when the ad text is fine.
steps.say: Review isn't a single gate. Follow the flow on screen. You submit an ad, automated systems review it, sometimes people do too, and it's approved or rejected. Then it can be checked again at any time while it's live, and you can appeal if you think a decision is wrong. So an ad approved yesterday can be rejected today. And reviews look at the landing page too, not just the ad itself.

steps.p: Most policies sort content into three buckets. Knowing which bucket your offer sits in is the first question to answer before you build any ad, page or funnel.
d: Allowed|normal rules apply
Restricted|allowed only with conditions: permission, age limits, certain countries
Prohibited|never allowed, no matter how it is worded
steps.say: Most policies sort content into three buckets. Look at the cards. Allowed content follows the normal rules. Restricted content is allowed only with conditions, like permission, age limits or certain countries. Prohibited content is never allowed, no matter how it's worded. Knowing which bucket your offer sits in is the first question to answer, before you build any ad, page or funnel.

steps.p: As an affiliate you are the advertiser in the platform's eyes. The ad runs from your account, so the responsibility for following the rules is yours, not only the brand's.

steps.h: Platform approval is not the law
steps.p: Two separate checks apply to every regulated campaign: the platform's policy and the law of the country you target. Passing one does not pass the other. You need both before you spend.
steps.say: Here's the key idea. Platform approval is not the law. Two separate checks apply to every regulated campaign: the platform's policy, and the law of the country you target. Passing one doesn't mean you pass the other. You need both, before you spend a single dollar.

steps.p: Platform policy decides whether the ad may run on that platform. Local law decides whether the product may be offered and promoted to people in that country at all.

a.title: Platform policy
items: Set by the ad platform
Decides if the ad runs
Breaking it: rejected ads, banned accounts

b.title: Local law
items: Set by the country or state
Decides if the product is legal to promote
Breaking it: legal and financial risk

steps.say: Compare the two columns. Platform policy is set by the ad platform, and it decides whether the ad may run there. Breaking it means rejected ads and banned accounts. Local law is set by the country or state, and it decides whether the product is legal to offer and promote to people there at all. Breaking it brings legal and financial risk.

steps.h: 18+ is the floor, not the target
steps.p: Gambling and most trading products are for adults only. In many places the minimum age is 18, and some places set it higher. Set your age targeting to match the strictest rule that applies.

d.s: Use the strictest age rule that applies

steps.more: Platforms that allow gambling ads typically require you to target only people above the legal age in that location, and your landing page and offer should say clearly that the product is for adults. Age targeting on ad platforms relies on what users tell the platform, so honest creatives matter too: never use content that appeals mainly to young people, such as cartoon styles or school themes, for adult products.
steps.say: Gambling and most trading products are for adults only. In many places the minimum age is eighteen, and some places set it higher. So eighteen plus is the floor, not the target. Set your age targeting to match the strictest rule that applies. And because age targeting relies on what users tell the platform, keep creatives honest too. Never use content that mainly appeals to young people, like cartoon styles or school themes, for adult products.

You spend nine hundred dollars and generate forty F T Ds, first time deposits, at thirty dollars each. That would have been twelve hundred dollars. But the network reviews the traffic and rejects all forty. So you earn nothing, and lose the full nine hundred.

steps.p: Example: the whole $900 is gone and the account now has a history the network and platform may remember. Checking the licence first would have taken an email.

steps.p: Regulated offers often require specific messages in ads or on landing pages. Even where not required, they build trust with the people you want as long-term customers.

steps.say: Regulated offers often require specific messages in ads or on landing pages. Look at the cards. An age notice, eighteen plus or the local legal age. A gambling message to play responsibly, with help resources where required. A risk warning that trading can lose money. And no guarantees, ever, of wins or profit. Even where they're not required, these messages build trust with the people you want as long-term customers.

steps.p: Trading and gambling carry real risk of losing money. Ads that hide that are misleading, usually against policy and in many places against the law.

items: Guaranteed daily profit
You cannot lose

b.title: Honest

steps.say: Trading and gambling carry a real risk of losing money. Ads that hide that are misleading, usually against policy, and in many places against the law. Compare the columns. Misleading lines promise guaranteed daily profit, say you can't lose, or promise to turn ten dollars into a thousand this week. Honest lines say trading involves risk of loss, invite people to learn how the platform works, and remind them to only use money they can afford to lose.

steps.p: Every email, phone number and Telegram username you collect belongs to a real person. Data protection laws in many countries give people rights over that data and put duties on anyone who collects it.

steps.say: Here's the starting point. Data belongs to people. Every email, phone number and Telegram username you collect belongs to a real person. Data protection laws in many countries give people rights over that data, and put duties on anyone who collects it. You hold it, they own it. So collect with permission, and use it with care.

steps.h: Consent the wrong and right way
steps.p: Consent means the person clearly agreed. Adding people to lists they never joined, or buying numbers from someone else, is not consent, and often breaks both law and platform rules.

a.title: Wrong way
items: Buying lead or phone lists
Adding people to groups without asking
Scraping numbers from other groups
No way to opt out

items: People join from your own ads
Clear explanation of what they get

Respect requests to delete

steps.say: Consent means the person clearly agreed. Compare the columns. The wrong way is buying lead or phone lists, adding people to groups without asking, scraping numbers from other groups, and giving no way to opt out. That's not consent, and it often breaks both law and platform rules. The right way is people joining from your own ads, a clear explanation of what they get, an easy way to leave, and respecting requests to delete.

steps.p: Before you add a field to a form, ask what you will do with it. If you cannot name a use, leave it out. Less data means less risk, a shorter form and less to protect.

Less data means less risk, a shorter form, and less to protect.

steps.p: Your ad account is where your business lives. If it is restricted, your campaigns stop. Platforms keep a record of each account's behaviour and use it to decide how much they trust you.

d.s: Trust is built slowly and lost quickly

steps.say: Account health is business health. Your ad account is where your business lives. If it's restricted, your campaigns stop. Platforms keep a record of each account's behaviour, and use it to decide how much they trust you. Trust is built slowly and lost quickly, so protect the account.

steps.p: Example: a winning ad set earns $15 profit a day after spend. The account is restricted for 10 days while you fix a policy problem. That is $150 of profit gone, plus the data the ad set had built. Prevention is cheaper.

lessons.title: Spotting scams and protecting yourself
objectives: By the end you can recognise common scams aimed at new affiliates.
By the end you can vet a network before sending real traffic.
By the end you can protect your logins, data and money.

steps.p: No single sign proves a network is good or bad, but patterns tell you a lot. Several red flags together are a reason to walk away.

a.title: Red flags
items: Payouts far above everyone else
Asks you to pay to join
Vague payment terms
Pushes you to scale before paying

b.title: Green flags
items: Payouts in line with the market
Written terms you can read
Pays the first invoice on time
Explains rejected conversions

steps.say: No single sign proves a network is good or bad, but patterns tell you a lot. Compare the columns. Red flags are payouts far above everyone else, asking you to pay to join, vague payment terms, and pushing you to scale before they've paid. Green flags are payouts in line with the market, written terms you can read, paying the first invoice on time, and explaining rejected conversions. Several red flags together are a reason to walk away.

steps.h: When a payout looks too good
steps.p: Example: three networks pay about $30 to $40 per FTD for the same brand and geo. A new one offers $120. That gap needs an explanation before you send a single click.

d.text: Ask why the payout is higher, what the qualification rules are and when the first payment happens. Then test with a small amount before trusting it.

steps.p: Example of a fake network message. It mixes a payout far above the market with a fee and a deadline. Any one of those is a reason to slow down. All three together is a reason to block.

What is your company name, and where are your written payment terms?

All three together is a reason to block, and the buyer does exactly that.

steps.h: Worked example: test a network's payment
steps.p: Example: you start small with a new network that pays weekly with a $100 threshold. You only scale once each payment arrives in full and on time.

steps.p: Most account takeovers start with a stolen password or a shared login. These steps are free and take less than an hour to set up.

A unique password for every account
A password manager to store them

quiz.q: A network asks you to pay $200 to access its best offers. What does this most likely signal?
options: A premium network
A normal industry fee
A red flag that it may be a scam
A sign of high payouts
quiz.why: Legitimate networks earn from the advertiser, not by charging affiliates to join.

quiz.q: You get a DM from "Meta Support" with a link to verify your account in 24 hours. What do you do?
options: Click quickly to save the account
Ignore the link and check your account inside the platform directly
Send them your password to speed it up
Forward it to your team to click
quiz.why: Real notices appear inside your account. Links in DMs pushing urgency are a common phishing trick.

quiz.q: Other networks pay $30 to $40 per FTD. A new one offers $120 for the same brand and geo. Best move?
options: Ask why, read the rules and test small before trusting it
Send all your traffic now
Ignore the other networks forever
Pay them a deposit to secure the rate
quiz.why: A payout far above market needs an explanation. Test with a small amount and confirm payment first.

quiz.q: Week 3 payment is late and the manager does not reply. What do you do?
options: Double the budget to earn more
Keep sending traffic as normal
Delete your records
Pause new spend and follow up until it is resolved
quiz.why: Stop growing what the network owes you until payment is resolved. That protects your bankroll if it is a scam.

quiz.q: Which is the safest way to give a media buyer access to your ad account?
options: Share your password
Share your password and two-factor code
Add them with their own role in your business portfolio
Let them log in from your phone
quiz.why: Roles give access without sharing your login, and you can remove them at any time.

exam.q: A network approves you for a gambling offer in Ghana. You have not checked Meta's gambling rules or the brand's licence there. What should you do first?
options: Launch a small test to see if ads approve
Run it from a friend's account to be safe
Use a page that shows reviewers a different offer
Confirm the brand's licence for Ghana and the platform authorization before launching
exam.why: Regulated offers need both a valid local licence and platform authorization. Testing first, borrowing accounts or cloaking all break the rules.

exam.q: Your lead form has a consent box that is ticked by default because it "converts better". What is the correct fix?
options: Leave the box empty so the person ticks it themselves, with the notice linked beside it
Keep it ticked but make the text smaller
Remove the box and the notice
Keep it ticked for trading offers only
exam.why: Consent is an active choice. A pre-ticked box is not consent in most privacy laws.

exam.q: An ad was approved last week. Today it is rejected for a landing page problem, though the ad text did not change. Why?
options: The platform made a random error
Ads and landing pages can be re-reviewed at any time while live
Approved ads cannot be rejected
The budget was too high
exam.why: Review continues while ads run, and the destination page is part of the review.

exam.q: A seller offers aged ad accounts "with high limits" for $150 each. What is the right view?
options: A smart way to scale faster
Fine if you only use them for testing
A breach of platform terms that can lead to losing linked assets
Allowed if the seller gives a receipt
exam.why: Buying or renting accounts breaks platform terms and can involve fraud. Build and protect your own account.

exam.q: You plan $40 a day for 5 days with a 25% buffer. How much should your card have available?
Your manager sends a link to a regulator page showing the brand is licensed in Kenya. What is the safest way to check?
options: Trust the link, it came from the manager
Ask for a screenshot instead
Check that the page looks official
Type the regulator's address yourself and search its register for the company and licence number
exam.why: Fake regulator pages exist. Opening the official site yourself and matching the company, number and status is the reliable check.

exam.q: Your landing page collects phone numbers but has no privacy notice. Which fix comes first?
options: Add a privacy notice saying what you collect and why, and ask consent where required
Hash the numbers so no notice is needed
Collect more data to improve matching
Move the form to Telegram so rules do not apply
exam.why: People must know what you collect and why. Hashing or changing the channel does not remove your privacy duties.

exam.q: An offer's weekly cap is 30 FTDs at $40. By Thursday you have 30. What do you do?
options: Keep spending, extra FTDs will be paid
Switch the traffic to a geo the offer does not list
Ask your manager in writing for a cap increase before sending more traffic
Send the extra traffic and argue later
exam.why: Conversions over the cap may not be paid. Get a written increase or pause until the cap resets.

exam.q: A creative uses a famous musician's face saying they use the app. You do not have permission. What is the problem?
options: None if it converts
Only a problem in Europe
It is fine if the video is AI generated
It is a fake endorsement: deceptive, banned and possibly illegal
exam.why: Using real people without permission to imply endorsement is deception, whether filmed or AI generated.

exam.q: A new network owes you $380, your exposure limit is $300 and payment is a week late. Best action?
options: Stop new spend with them and follow up until they pay
Increase spend to show commitment
Ignore your limit this once
Delete your tracking so they cannot dispute it
exam.why: You are already over your limit with a late payment. Stop growing the exposure and resolve the payment first.
